evidence: Anatomy of a Seance (5 citations) is catalogued under Stanley Edward McMullin and described as Stan McMullin's work. Massanoga (1), coauthored with Robert Stacey, also credits Stan McMullin. Stan is the shortened name of the LC author.

Byzantinoturcica (5 citations) is by Gyula Moravcsik. He also contributed to the 1962 De administrando imperio: Commentary (1), whose published review lists Gy. Moravcsik among its authors. Gy. abbreviates Gyula.

All 6 citations concern the 1969 Favelas do Rio de Janeiro: Evolucao, sentido. WorldCat attributes this exact book to Luciano Parisse; scholarly discussion calls its author Lucien Parisse. The differing given names refer to the author of the same work.

Vice in Chicago (6 citations) is by Walter C. Reckless. The publisher also credits Walter C. Reckless for The Impact of War on Crime, Delinquency, and Prostitution (1942; 1). The bibliography's middle initial T is erroneous for both titles.

Charlotte Roueche's research biography explicitly identifies both Performers and Partisans at Aphrodisias (1993; 6 citations) and Aphrodisias in Late Antiquity (1989; 1) as her books. Ch. abbreviates Charlotte.

All 6 citations concern Radio Nacional: o Brasil em Sintonia, by Luiz Carlos Saroldi and Sonia Virginia Moreira. The library record uses both Luis Carlos and Luiz Carlos for this author; Luis/Luiz is a spelling variation here.

Domicide (5 citations) is coauthored by Sandra E. Smith; its publisher preview identifies her as Sandra Eileen Smith, 1942-. Charlotte Hawkins Brown (1982; 1; DOI 10.2307/2294689) is credited to Sandra N. Smith in JSTOR. The LC author's share is 5/6.

Yale University Press identifies Steve Tibble as author of both Monarchy and Lordships in the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem, 1099-1291 (5 citations) and The Crusader Armies, 1099-1187 (1). Steven and Steve identify the same author of these works.

Tissue Economies (5 citations) is by Catherine Waldby and Robert Mitchell; The Biopolitics of Reproduction (1) is by Catherine Waldby and Melinda Cooper. Cathy is a catalogued name variant. The zero-citation Destruction fragment also matches Catherine Waldby's chapter in Sexy Bodies (1995).

All 5 citations concern A Treatise on Adulterations of Food and Culinary Poisons (1820). Princeton's published historical account identifies its author as Frederick Accum (1769-1838), originally Friedrich; the Science History Institute catalogues the title under Friedrich Christian Accum.
